module_title: Hybrid Networking, Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect

scenes.title: VPN CloudHub: remote site mesh through a VGW
scenes.visual_overview: The original slide explains vpn cloudhub: remote site mesh through a vgw using 4 explicitly labelled visual sections, connections, and practical limits.
visual_walkthrough: Multiple site-to-site VPN connections share one virtual private gateway
Distinct customer ASNs, BGP and nonoverlapping remote prefixes
The VGW can re-advertise learned routes among remote sites
CloudHub does not give VPC peering transit; contrast Transit Gateway
scenes.visual_example: A corporate design joins three remote sites through a central VGW and must explicitly verify learned remote routes and return traffic.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Validate the vpn cloudhub: remote site mesh through a vgw design with supported network settings, complete traffic paths and its actual failure domains.
scenes.narration: This lesson explains vpn cloudhub: remote site mesh through a vgw, using the actual architecture and numbered callouts on the screen. Start with the first element: Multiple site-to-site VPN connections share one virtual private gateway. Notice the depicted connections and boundaries; they illustrate which component owns this responsibility. Next, follow the second section: Distinct customer ASNs, BGP and nonoverlapping remote prefixes. This changes how the path or control is configured, and should be checked rather than assumed. Move to the third section: The VGW can re-advertise learned routes among remote sites. For a working design, distinguish a successful control-plane configuration from application-level reachability, security and service readiness. Now inspect the final section: CloudHub does not give VPC peering transit; contrast Transit Gateway. Consider a realistic architecture scenario. A corporate design joins three remote sites through a central VGW and must explicitly verify learned remote routes and return traffic. When troubleshooting, test the forward and return paths, the relevant service-specific limits and actual user traffic, then compare the result with the requirement. The key takeaway is to select the correct model and prove its behaviour under normal operation and failure.

scenes.title: Client VPN: split tunnel versus full tunnel
scenes.visual_overview: The original slide explains client vpn: split tunnel versus full tunnel using 4 explicitly labelled visual sections, connections, and practical limits.
visual_walkthrough: Split tunnel installs relevant client routes, leaving other internet traffic outside the VPN
Full tunnel sends client traffic toward the VPN and requires deliberate internet egress
Access to peered or on-premises networks needs complete routes, authorization and return path
Transit Gateway integration follows its supported endpoint-specific model and access limitations
scenes.visual_example: A remote employee should use full tunnel only when centralized internet inspection is required and the VPN-side egress is provisioned.

scenes.title: Direct Connect SiteLink: site-to-site transport
scenes.visual_overview: The original slide explains direct connect sitelink: site-to-site transport using 4 explicitly labelled visual sections, connections, and practical limits.
visual_walkthrough: SiteLink allows eligible on-premises sites to exchange traffic via Direct Connect locations
Enable SiteLink on eligible private or transit VIFs attached to the same Direct Connect gateway
The site-to-site path can bypass Region transit, subject to routing and WAN policy
SiteLink does not remove last-mile failures or encrypt applications automatically
scenes.visual_example: Two offices in different colocation sites can exchange routes through SiteLink, but must separately secure traffic and protect last-mile access.
